summary.text: A substitution reaction is a chemical reaction in which one functional group in a compound is replaced by another.
Substitution reactions are of prime importance in organic chemistry, and understanding a reaction type helps predict its product.
Nucleophilic substitution runs by two mechanisms: S_N1 in two steps and S_N2 in a single step.

facts.label: Also called
facts.value: Single displacement or single substitution reaction

facts.label: S_N1 steps
facts.value: Leaving group departs, then the nucleophile attaches

facts.label: S_N2 steps
facts.value: One step, with attack and departure happening together

facts.label: S_N2 outcome
facts.value: Always inverts configuration, called a Walden inversion

facts.label: Rate laws
facts.value: S_N1 is first-order and S_N2 is second-order

items.prompt: A reagent attacks a carbon and the old group leaves at the very same moment, all in one step. Which mechanism is this?
items.explain: In S_N2 the attack of the reagent and the expulsion of the leaving group happen simultaneously.

items.prompt: A leaving group sits on a carbon crowded with bulky groups, which block an attack from behind. Which route does the substitution take?
items.explain: Steric crowding, such as at a tertiary carbon, makes the substitution go by S_N1 rather than S_N2.

items.prompt: A chemist wants to tune the temperature and solvent of a reaction to get more product. Why does knowing the reaction type help?

options.label: It makes the temperature and solvent matter less
It helps predict the product and optimize variables like these
It fixes the product no matter what is changed
It shows which reactions can skip the leaving group

items.explain: Detailed understanding of a reaction type helps predict the outcome and optimize variables such as temperature and solvent.

items.prompt: A leaving group departs from a chiral carbon, leaving a carbocation, and then a nucleophile attaches. What happens to the stereochemistry?

options.label: It always keeps the same configuration
It is always destroyed and cannot be tracked
Inversion or retention can occur, usually with no preference

items.explain: The two-step mechanism can give inversion or retention, and usually both occur without preference.

items.prompt: Light splits chlorine gas into chlorine radicals, and one of them meets methane. One breaks a C–H bond and takes the hydrogen. What forms in the end?
items.explain: One radical grabs a hydrogen to form HCl, and the other bonds with the CH₃ group to form methyl chloride.

items.prompt: A nucleophile attacks a carbon that is double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to another atom, so the double bond breaks and then reforms. What kind of substitution is this?
items.explain: Acyl substitution happens when a nucleophile attacks a carbon double-bonded to one oxygen and single-bonded to another; the double bond reforms and kicks off the leaving group.
